text.p: Worldwide semiconductor revenues fell 7 percent to $141 billion in 1996, market research firm Dataquest said Tuesday.
It attributed the decline to a steep drop in the market for dynamic random access memory (DRAM) chips, the most common type of computer memory chip.

The semiconductor market suffered in 1996 as the average selling price for DRAMs fell by three-fourths, Dataquest said. It said that excluding DRAMs, the 1996 semiconductor market grew by 6 percent, led by a 14 percent microcomponent revenue growth.
Intel Corp. remained the world's No.1 chip producer, gaining momentum with 29 percent growth in revenues. It had overall market share of 12 percent in 1996, Dataquest said.

Intel's 1996 revenues of about $16.9 billion were nearly $6 billion more than those of second-place NEC Corp., which saw a 6 percent decline in revenues. NEC had 7.5 percent market share, Dataquest said.
Motorola Inc.'s revenues dropped 3 percent to $8.4 billion, leaving it with a 6 percent market share.
Intel and SGS-Thomson Microelectronics NV were alone among the top nine producers to record revenue gains.

Japanese and Korean companies, with the exception of NEC, saw double-digit 1996 revenue declines of 12 to 26 percent. Those companies included Hitachi Ltd, Toshiba Corp., Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd and Fujitsu Ltd.
Hitachi had 5.7 percent market share after revenues fell 12 percent to $8 billion, Dataquest said. Toshiba also had 5.7 percent market share, with revenues off 21 percent to $7.9 billion.
Samsung's revenues fell 26 percent to $6.2 billion, leaving it with 4.4 percent market share. Fujitsu's revenues were down 19 percent to $4.5 billion, giving it a 3.2 percent market share.
European chip producer SGS-Thomson's revenues rose 24 percent to $4.2 billion, giving it a 3 percent market share.
Dataquest said Texas Instruments Inc.'s revenues dropped 9 percent to $7 billion, leaving it with a market share of 5 percent.
